abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: A large body of evidence has highlighted the role of non-coding RNAs in neurodevelopment and neuroinflammation. This evidence has led to increasing speculation that non-coding RNAs may be involved in the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying hydrocephalus, one of the most common neurological conditions worldwide. In this review, we first outline the basic concepts and incidence of hydrocephalus along with the limitations of existing treatments for this condition. Then, we outline the definition, classification, and biological role of non-coding RNAs. Subsequently, we analyze the roles of non-coding RNAs in the formation of hydrocephalus in detail. Specifically, we have focused on the potential significance of non-coding RNAs in the pathophysiology of hydrocephalus, including glymphatic pathways, neuroinflammatory processes, and neurological dysplasia, on the basis of the existing evidence. Lastly, we review the potential of non-coding RNAs as biomarkers of hydrocephalus and for the creation of innovative treatments.

sec.p: Keywords: hydrocephalus, neurodevelopment, neuroinflammation, non-coding RNA, therapeutic target

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Hydrocephalus, in which an imbalance in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) homeostasis causes the ventricles to fill with CSF, is one of the most prevalent neurological conditions worldwide (Karimy et al., 2020). However, some forms of hydrocephalus, such as idiopathic intracranial hypertension, do not present with ventriculomegaly (Hladky and Barrand, 2024). Hydrocephalus can be caused by congenital dysplasia and genetic factors and is often secondary to a variety of central nervous system (CNS) diseases, such as tumors, subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), traumatic brain injury (TBI), and intracranial infection (Karim et al., 2020; Müller-Schmitz et al., 2020; Whitehead and Weiner, 2022). The two most common forms of hydrocephalus worldwide are post-infectious hydrocephalus (PIH) induced by CNS infections and post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (PHH) caused by IVH (Holste et al., 2022; Thompson et al., 2022). Regardless of etiology, hydrocephalus usually presents with disorientation and headache, urinary incontinence, vision and sleep disturbances, gait abnormalities, and cognitive and developmental changes, which can progress to coma, neurological decline, and death if not treated promptly (Hochstetler et al., 2022).

A recent meta-analysis showed that the mean prevalence of hydrocephalus was 85/100,000, with the prevalences in children, adults, and older adults being 88/100,000, 11/100,000, and 175/100,000, respectively (Isaacs et al., 2018). Moreover, the incidence of different types of hydrocephalus shows regional differences. Among pediatric cases of hydrocephalus, PHH accounts for most cases in developed countries while PIH accounts for more than 80% of the cases in low- and middle-income countries. This difference is primarily attributable to the lack of well-established neonatal intensive care conditions in low-income countries, which results in low survival rates among premature infants (Kahle et al., 2024). The estimated cost of treatment of hydrocephalus in children alone is US$2 billion annually, which represents a significant financial burden (Kahle et al., 2016). Moreover, reliable data on the incidence and burden of hydrocephalus in adults are lacking, necessitating further epidemiological investigation (Dewan et al., 2018).

The existing internationally accepted surgical treatment strategies for hydrocephalus include ventriculo-peritoneal shunting and endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) (Dhandapani et al., 2021). Choroid plexus cauterization in conjunction with ETV has been demonstrated to increase the effectiveness of ETV in infant patients (Kahle et al., 2016). Regrettably, however, shunt therapy is associated with a range of complications, such as infection, mechanical obstruction, tubing complications, various types of intracranial hemorrhages, shunt ascites, and perforated infection of hollow internal organs (Kumar et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021a). ETV surgery is also not absolutely safe, and may be associated with complications such as subcortical brain abscess, status epilepticus, Terson syndrome (retinal hemorrhage), and acute subdural hematoma (Grand et al., 2016). Moreover, medical treatment does not yield optimistic outcomes for hydrocephalus. Some drugs, such as acetazolamide and furosemide, have been shown to be associated with higher shunt placement rates and increased neurological morbidity in infants with PHH and are therefore not recommended. Thus, to create more potent treatment approaches, more detailed investigation of the disease pathophysiology is essential.

Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), which are functional RNAs that do not encode proteins, account for about 98%–99% of all RNAs in the mammalian genome and play important roles in human growth and development by coordinating cellular functions (Beermann et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2024; Knight et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). NcRNAs have been shown to regulate transcription and translation biologically via means of sponges, RNA/protein scaffolds, and epigenetic alterations in both pathological and healthy settings (Mehta et al., 2021). Different cellular life processes involve different kinds of ncRNAs. Among the different types of ncRNAs, microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), and circular RNAs (circRNAs) have been shown to be associated with pathophysiological mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic targets of hydrocephalus and its related diseases.

MiRNAs are small regulatory RNAs extracted from the stem-loop region of longer RNA transcripts (Sharma et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). They are roughly 22 nucleotides long (Bartel, 2018). MiRNAs recognize and bind to the 3′ untranslated region (3′ UTR) of the target mRNA through their own “seed sequence,” the base sequence between the second and eighth nucleotides that can be complementary to the target mRNA (Lee et al., 2020). They inhibit protein expression mainly by inducing mRNA degradation and inhibiting the initiation of translation (He and Hannon, 2004).

LncRNAs, which are longer than 200 nucleotides, have historically been regarded as “noise” in transcription. Like mRNA, they are widely present in different tissues, and most are expressed in the brain (Ponting et al. 2009). LncRNA function is often achieved through one of the following mechanisms: (1) epigenetic modification or regulation of epigenetic modification by recruiting chromatin regulatory proteins that upregulate or inhibit transcriptional activity; (2) changing the expression and function of splicing factors and affecting the pre-mRNA splicing process; and (3) communication between competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs), such as lncRNAs or circRNAs, to achieve regulation of gene expression by competing for binding to shared miRNAs or mRNAs (Tay et al., 2014). lncRNAs can directly bind to mRNAs or miRNAs through base-complementary pairing and regulate gene expression or act as ceRNAs for miRNAs (Chen et al., 2021b; Liu et al., 2023).

CircRNAs are spatiotemporally specific and highly conserved, difficult to degrade by RNA exonucleases, and widely expressed in eukaryotes (Hanan et al., 2017). circRNAs are generated upon reverse splicing of pre-mRNA, which means that one or more exons are joined to the upstream 3′ splice site in the opposite order through the downstream 5′ splice site (Chen, 2020). circRNAs are functionally diverse and can bind to DNA or snRNA to regulate transcriptional activity, act as ceRNAs or miR sponges to regulate gene expression, and can also be translated into proteins (Zhou et al., 2020). An increasing number of experimental studies have highlighted the influence of circRNAs on different diseases (van Zonneveld et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023).

The potential of ncRNAs in biomarker development and targeted therapy for hydrocephalus and related diseases is being increasingly recognized. Nevertheless, the present body of literature does not include an examination of the connection between ncRNAs and hydrocephalus. Therefore, we have attempted to systematically elaborate the pathophysiological mechanisms of ncRNAs involved in hydrocephalus in order to explore effective biomarkers and treatment strategies.

sec.title: Retrieval Strategy
sec.p: A computer-based online search of the PubMed database was performed to retrieve articles published up to October 6, 2024. The following text terms (MeSH terms) were combined in order to optimize search sensitivity and specificity: “hydrocephalus,” “post-infectious hydrocephalus,” “non-coding RNA,” “ncRNA,” “choroid plexus,” “ependyma,” “TOLL like receptor,” “NLRP3 inflammasome,” “AQP4,” “glymphatic pathway,” “biomarkers,” “intraventricular hemorrhage,” “subarachnoid haemorrhage,” “neuroinflammation,” and “treatment.” After additional screening of the results on the basis of titles and abstracts, only publications examining the connection between ncRNAs and hydrocephalus and related illnesses were included in our analysis of the relationship between ncRNAs and hydrocephalus. No restrictions related to the study type or language were applied in the search. Only hydrocephalus-related articles that did not also evaluate ncRNAs were excluded.

sec.title: Mechanisms of Non-Coding RNAs Involved in Hydrocephalus Formation
Non-coding RNAs involved in hydrocephalus formation
sec.p: The role of ncRNAs has been thoroughly investigated and understood. miRNAs are widely involved in controlling life processes like differentiation, apoptosis, and proliferation. They are also crucial in the development of cancers, cardiovascular disorders, and neurological disorders (Esteller, 2011). LncRNAs have a wide range of functions, including subcellular structural organization, telomere biology, higher-order chromosomal dynamics, and biological processes (Mercer et al., 2009). LncRNAs have been shown to have some effects on CNS diseases, tumors and hematologic disorders (Mercer et al., 2009; Policarpo et al., 2021). CircRNAs are abundant in mammalian brains and are highly enriched in synapses. circRNAs are highly conserved in expression and, therefore, show evolutionary conservation in terms of location within the brain and developmental timing. Their role in CNS disease pathogenesis and disease interventions is also being increasingly recognized (Rybak-Wolf et al., 2015).

Patients with hydrocephalus show considerably different miRNA expression profiles. Exosomes were extracted from the CSF of neonates with PHH in 2019 by Spaull et al., who also found a noteworthy increase in miR-1911-5p expression after the onset of PHH. In 2022, Chen et al. were the first to report exosomal miRNA expression profiles in congenital hydrocephalus (CH). Patients with CH showed 31 highly expressed exosomal miRNAs, of which 26 were upregulated and five were downregulated. Through Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis and the prediction of differentially produced exosomal miRNA target mRNA, they demonstrated that hsa-miR-130b-3p binds PTEN to perform biological functions (Chen et al., 2022). In contrast, Pten has been shown to be associated with CH, and deletion of Pten has been shown to lead to hydrocephalus in mice (Ohtoshi, 2008). Thus, hsa-miR-130b-3p may be crucial for the formation of CH through its effects on PTEN.

Another topic of interest is that the onset of hydrocephalus may be accompanied by a comparable alteration in lncRNA expression patterns. A recent bioinformatics study that used high-throughput sequencing technology to analyze C57BL6/J mice with kaolin-induced hydrocephalus showed significant differences in lncRNA and mRNA expression profiles in the C57BL/6 group in comparison with the mice in the saline group (Shi et al., 2019). The majority of lncRNAs are involved in pathways regulated by five key transcription factors (TFs), namely, BPTF, FOXM1, NR5A2, P2RX5, and NR6A1. This finding raises the possibility that these TFs are associated with the development of hydrocephalus. In addition, GO and KEGG analysis suggest that the complement and coagulation cascades, the hypoxia inducible factor-1 and chemokine signaling pathways, phagosomes, and the mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathway may be essential in the development of hydrocephalus (Shi et al., 2019).

Non-coding RNAs, including microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs, play an important role in the regulation of disease and health in various tissues and organs. Non-coding RNAs can regulate the fibrosis and immune processes of the cardiovascular, lung, and kidney systems, as well as the proliferation and metastasis of tumors. In the central nervous system, non-coding RNAs mediate the development of hydrocephalus through mechanisms such as choroid plexus developmental defects, the glymphatic pathway, aquaporin 4 (AQP4) dysfunction, and neuroinflammation.

sec.title: Defects in central nervous system and choroid plexus development
sec.p: Existing studies have suggested that some mutations related to neurogenesis and development lead to defects in the mutual regulation of this gene and target ncRNAs, resulting in impaired ciliary cell and fetal neurogliogenesis in the CNS, which in turn causes hydrocephalus (LaSalle et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2022a). Let-7, one of the first miRNAs identified, is an essential regulator of cell differentiation. It can bind to the Trim71 3′ UTR to inhibit the translation of Trim71. In the ciliated neuroepithelium, Trim71 is strongly expressed, whereas let-7 miRNA and Trim71 antagonize each other (Cuevas et al., 2015). This double-negative feedback loop controls normal neural tube development and proliferation, destiny specification, and/or differentiation of neural progenitor cells (NPCs) (Liu et al., 2021c). Three de novo mutations in Trim71 have been reported in four individuals with CH. Notably, all three de novo mutations occur at three homologous sites in the RNA-binding NHL domain. This causes neural stem cell (NSC) niche depletion and premature neural development (Welte et al., 2019). Since neurogenesis and gliogenesis are impaired, the cerebral cortex becomes thinner, which, in turn, causes ventriculomegaly and produces CH (Furey et al., 2018). On the basis of this evidence, we hypothesize that ncRNAs may act with neuropili or neurodevelopment-related genes and thus have some relevance to the development of CH. However, direct experimental evidence linking neurodevelopment and neurociliary defects and hydrocephalus is limited, and further studies are needed to support this view.

In addition, the loss of some miRNAs can lead to defects in choroid plexus development and dysfunction. CSF is largely produced by a single layer of cuboidal cells of the choroid plexus epithelium. In cooperation with several integral membrane proteins, water and ions travel throughout epithelial cells, thereby controlling CSF synthesis and secretion (Damkier et al., 2013). Different signaling cascades affect these channels, changing their transport functions and, in turn, the passage of solutes and water through them. Targeting the TF E2f5, miRNA-449 is particularly expressed in the developing choroid plexus of mouse embryos as well as in the epithelial cell layer of the adult choroid plexus (Redshaw et al., 2009). In 1998, Lindeman et al. showed that homozygous E2F-5 mice developed hydrocephalus and confirmed that the pathogenesis of this hydrocephalus involved excess CSF production by the choroid plexus. E2f5 is dynamically expressed in embryonic development and regulates the development and maturation of choroid plexus epithelial cells (CPes). Moreover, as a TF, it regulates signaling cascades and affects the transepithelial transport of water and ions, thereby inhibiting CSF secretion (Swetloff and Ferretti, 2005).

Dysfunction of cilia on the surface of ependymal epithelial cells can lead to excessive intraventricular CSF accumulation, which is considered an important pathophysiological mechanism underlying hydrocephalus (Ji et al., 2022).. Clinical studies and animal models of CH have suggested that ependymal motile cilia are essential for the movement of CSF (Kumar et al., 2021; Duy et al., 2022). On each ependymal cell, approximately 50 cilia assist in guiding CSF flow through the ventricular system (Ji et al., 2022). Motile cilia from the ependymal lining beat spontaneously, providing effective pressure to regulate CSF flow, maintain normal circulation of CSF in the ventricles, and prevent excessive accumulation of CSF in the ventricles (Olstad et al., 2019). Previous research has demonstrated the significant regulatory functions of ncRNAs in ciliogenesis (Cao et al., 2012; Alanazi et al., 2024). By controlling important molecules in the signaling pathways connected to ciliogenesis, miRNAs can contribute to the pathophysiological process of hydrocephalus. The miR-449 family (miR-499a, miR-499b, and miR-499c) has been shown to substantially influence the development of epithelial cells and is significantly enriched in multi-ciliated cells (Loukas et al., 2021). The progenitor cells of multi-ciliated cells express miR-449, which directly causes suppression of cell cycle components and inhibits the Delta/Notch pathway, leading to cell cycle arrest and entry into terminal differentiation (Marcet et al., 2011. Wu et al. (2014) reported that the miR-34b/c and miR-449 clusters have functional redundancy. Unbiased bioinformatics analysis showed that these two miRNA clusters regulate 239 target mRNAs that are essential for biological processes such as brain development and motile ciliogenesis. The Dgcr8-miR-382-3p and miR-674-3p-Drd1 pathways regulate ciliary beating and ventricular volume homeostasis in ependymal cells, in accordance with recent findings obtained by Eom et al. (2020). In Dgcr8-haploinsufficient mice, expression of miR-382-3p and miR-674-3p was markedly negatively regulated (Eom et al., 2020). By directly or indirectly limiting the expression levels of genes relevant to the cell cycle, centrioles, and cilia (e.g., CDC20B), miR-34/449 controls multiciliogenesis (Revinski et al., 2018). According to a different study, TAp73 and miRNA-449 cooperate to promote multiciliogenesis and the development of the choroid plexus (Wildung et al., 2019). The ciliary tissue in the choroid plexus is reduced when miRNA-449 is lost alone, while multiciliogenesis in the choroid plexus is significantly reduced when TAp73 and miRNA-449 are both absent (Wildung et al., 2019). This experimental evidence broadly suggests that miRNA-449 is associated with motile cilia development in ependymal cells. Moreover, defects in ciliary development have been shown to be highly associated with hydrocephalus (Ji et al., 2022); thus, we hypothesize that miRNA-449 also contributes to the formation of hydrocephalus; however, more research is required to validate this hypothesis. The 3′ UTR of Drd1 is the target of miR-382-3p and miR-674-3p, which control the expression of Drd1. Their disappearance raises ependymal cell levels of Drd1, which results in reduced ciliary activity, ventricular dilatation, and hydrocephalus (Eom et al., 2020). Evidence for other ncRNAs is limited, and the existing experimental evidence has only shown that the lncRNA Trincr1 can specifically recognize the RNA motif of TRIM71 (mTRIM71) and thus interact with it (Shi et al., 2024). The effect of TRIM71 in CH has been described previously.

In summary, miRNAs can affect CSF circulation by (1) regulating CNS development and (2) directly or indirectly regulating choroid plexus ciliogenesis-related pathways and regulating choroid plexus development. Hydrocephalus can arise as a result of aberrant CSF accumulation in the ventricles as a result of mutations or deletions in miRNAs and the target genes linked to them. Conclusions regarding lncRNAs and circRNAs, on the other hand, cannot be obtained due to the paucity of relevant literature, and we look forward to more in-depth studies on this topic.

sec.title: Pyrin domain-containing protein 3 inflammasome
sec.p: As mentioned earlier, both intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and TBI can lead to the occurrence of hydrocephalus, and the underlying molecular mechanisms are not clear. The functions of the pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome in PHH have increasingly come to light in recent years (Xiao et al., 2020; Shaik et al., 2023). The NLRP3 inflammasome, an important innate immunity regulator, is triggered in response to cellular disruptions caused by infection and sterile damage (Banerjee et al., 2022). Assembly of the NLRP3 inflammasomes activates caspase-1, which promotes cell lysis and elicits inflammatory responses through maturation and release of interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18 (Xu and Núñez, 2023). ICH and TBI have been reported to activate NLRP3 inflammasomes, and the resultant production of caspase-1 activates IL-1β and IL-18, favoring neutrophil infiltration and thereby exacerbating the inflammatory response (O’Brien et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2020). After IVH, the ventricles’ red blood cells lyse, releasing hemoglobin, iron, peroxiredoxin-2, and carbonic anhydrase-1, which in turn causes inflammation in the choroid plexus (Holste et al., 2022). The choroidal transporter Na+/K+/2Cl ion co-transporter (NKCC1) is upregulated after IVH and SAH, and Na+/K+-ATPase activity is also elevated. These changes ultimately result in CSF hypersecretion, ventriculomegaly, and an unusual accumulation of water in the brain (Lolansen et al., 2022). Zhang et al. (2022a) demonstrated that NLRP3 activation in macrophages and microglia is inextricably linked to the pathophysiology of PHH and causes subependymal edema and cognitive impairment during ICH-IVH. These lines of evidence inevitably led us to consider the possibility of a link between NLRP3 inflammasome activation and hemorrhagic hydrocephalus.

Until the study by Zhang et al. (2022b) unveiled the mystery for us, inhibition of NLRP3 by MCC950 or NLRP3 knockout decreased phosphorylation of NKCC1, altered Na+- and K+-coupled water transport to regulate CSF secretion, reduced ventricular dilation and the development of PHH. Specifically, adenosine triphosphate, one of the damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), triggers P2X7 receptors and causes K+ efflux following bleeding. Under the influence of an electrochemical propellant, Cl– is concurrently effluxed (Chen et al., 2013). Variations in the levels of intracellular K+ and Cl– ions trigger the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. This, in turn, triggers the activation of caspase-1, pro-IL-1b (p-IL-1b), and pro-IL-18 (p-IL-18) as well as NKCC1, which results in the hypersecretion of CSF (Wang et al., 2020; Koumangoye, 2022). Therefore, modulating the development of hydrocephalus by regulating the NLRP3 inflammasome is particularly worthy of attention.

Recent studies have shown that ncRNAs, especially miRNAs, are critical for regulating the NLRP3 inflammasome’s activity after ICH (Boxberger et al., 2019). In this regard, some miRNAs directly target the non-coding region of NLRP3, repress its transcription, and downregulate NLRP3 expression. For instance, after ICH, miR-223 inhibits NLRP3 production via binding sites in the NLRP3 3′ UTR, which reduces microglial inflammation and neuronal damage (Yang et al., 2015). Similarly, miR-29a-5p has been demonstrated to lower the expression levels of NLRP3, pro-caspase-1, and cleaved caspase-1 in the brain tissues of TBI model mice and to prevent NLRP3 expression and activation (Zhang et al., 2021). Furthermore, miRNAs regulate NLRP3-related pathways and indirectly inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation. miR-124-3p and miR-194-5p have the ability to target the 3′ UTR of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6) (Fang and Hong, 2021; Wan et al., 2021). Previous research has shown a significant connection between TRAF6 and the beginning, synthesis, and subsequent reactions of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Xing et al., 2017; Hou et al., 2021). TRAF6 induces NLRP3 oligomerization by engaging toll-like receptors (TLRs) or IL-1R-mediated non-transcriptional priming signals. More significantly, TRAF6 mediates pre-synthesized IL-18 secretion and particularly increases caspase-1 cleavage and pyroptosis that is triggered by TLR/IL-1R (Xing et al., 2017). Consequently, miR-124-3p and miR-194-5p inhibit downstream inflammatory responses by blocking the TRAF6-mediated inflammasome activation caused by NLRP3. Furthermore, miR-152 can shield against ICH-induced neuroinflammation and brain damage by preventing thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP)-induced NLRP3 activation (Hu et al., 2020). Previous experiments have shown that TXNIP expression is markedly increased following the onset of SAH (Zhao et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2019). Furthermore, the NLRP3 inflammasome-binding protein TXNIP promotes IL-1β and caspase-1 maturation in addition to facilitating the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Zhou et al., 2010). However, additional animal experiments and clinical evidence are required to determine whether these two targeted forms of regulation are directly associated with NLRP3-mediated increased CSF secretion.

The role of lncRNAs in regulating NLRP3 should likewise not be underestimated. lncRNAs can achieve regulation of NLRP3 inflammasomes from different locations in cells, e.g., by participating in chromosome modification, interfering with transcriptional and translational events, and modifying mRNA stability (Menon and Hua, 2020). Specifically, lncRNAs function similarly to ceRNAs in the pathophysiology of hydrocephalus. In TBI, lncRNA-Meg3 directly binds miR-7a-5p, thereby increasing NLRP3-mediated microglial inflammation (Meng et al., 2021). Lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-treated rat hippocampus tissue and microglial cell models showed that miR-138-5p-targeted lncRNA 4344 increased NLRP3 expression along with its downstream caspase-1, IL-1β, and IL-18 (Feng et al., 2021). On the basis of this evidence, lncRNAs can be reasonably considered to modulate NLRP3 inflammasome activation by targeting miRNAs. However, further studies are required to determine their contributions to hydrocephalus.

sec.title: TLR/NF-κB signaling pathway
sec.p: TLRs are essential for the development of post-hemorrhagic and post-infarctive hypotension. TLRs recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), conserved microbial compounds that trigger host defense mechanisms and are also known as pattern recognition receptors (Fitzgerald and Kagan, 2020). TLRs can be classified into cell surface and intracellular TLRs. Cell surface TLRs primarily identify microbial components of the membrane and cause inflammatory responses, whereas intracellular TLRs primarily identify bacterial or viral nucleic acids generated from microorganisms and cause type I IFN responses and responses to inflammation (Duan et al., 2022). As previously stated, CPes are the primary producers of CSF. The blood–cerebrospinal fluid barrier, between which CPes form the interface, is the immune system’s initial line of defense against pathogenic chemicals flowing in the bloodstream. Furthermore, the CSF environment is stabilized by this barrier. More importantly, CPes are involved in peripheral immune signal transmission to the brain and immune cell circulation within the neurological system. Like other epithelial cells, CPes express TLRs on their surface. Except for TLR8, all TLR gene transcripts were detected in CPes in animal experiments, and individual variations were noted (Skipor et al., 2015). Expression of TLR1, TLR2, TLR3, and TLR4 mRNA has also been observed in the choroid plexus of normal neonates (Stridh et al., 2013). PAMPs in the CSF, including bacterial LPS and viruses, viral nucleic acid components, and parasites, regulate TLR mRNA expression and activate them, causing non-specific innate immune responses (Laflamme and Rivest, 2001; Wojtkowiak-Giera et al., 2016; Hollidge et al., 2021). PAMPs specifically attach to TLR4 on the epithelial surface of CPes, forming a stable dimeric structure that tightly binds the TIR domain of TLR to myeloid differentiation primary reactive protein (MyD88) and toll/interleukin-1 receptor-domain-containing adaptor protein (Latty et al., 2018). IL-1 receptor-associated kinases (IRAKs), which include IRAK-M, IRAK4, IRAK1, and IRAK-2, are bound by MyD88. Together, these IRAKs constitute the Myddosome complex. IRAK1/2 and IRAK4 further trigger TRAF6, an E3 ubiquitin ligase. In this process, the tumor growth factor-β-activated protein kinase 1 complex is induced and activated. Activated tumor growth factor-β-activated protein kinase 1 phosphorylates and stimulates the IKK complex, causing the production of the activator NF-kB (Duan et al., 2022). When nuclear NF-κB activation promotes the production of inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α, Ste20-type stress kinase (SPAK) is triggered. The NKCC1 is phosphorylated by SPAK, increasing the transporter’s activity (Karimy et al., 2020). NKCC1 induces post-infection hydrocephalus through its inherent ability to synergistically transport water and by targeting ionic translocation in a manner independent of osmotic drive, causing an increase in the net production of CSF (Steffensen et al., 2018). TLRs also play an important role in PHH. Like PAMPs, a series of DAMPs such as metHgb generated after bleeding can also activate the TLR-MyD88-NF-κB pathway and SPAK-NKCC1 co-transporter complex, thereby triggering the formation of PHH (Karimy et al., 2017). Apart from CPes, microglia in the choroid plexus serve as immunological sentinels in the brain and express a broad range of TLRs constitutively. Furthermore, TLRs in microglial membranes can bind to DAMPs and PAMPs in circulating CSF, inducing microglial inflammatory responses and causing the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Through their binding to CPe cell receptors, they can further increase CPe inflammation and cause CSF hypersecretion (Karimy et al., 2020).

NcRNAs have been recently shown to be essential for controlling TLR signal transduction and gene expression (Nahid et al., 2011). Numerous studies have demonstrated that TLR expression and various signaling pathway components—such as TFs, regulatory molecules, signaling proteins, and cytokines—are regulated by ncRNAs, which are essential elements of intricate immune regulatory networks (Bayraktar et al., 2019; Ghafouri-Fard et al., 2021). MiRNAs are the most traditional non-coding RNAs and rely on TLR-induced expression of mitogen-activated protein kinase and NF-κB pathways upon pathogen invasion. Nevertheless, they also regulate TLR expression, TLR-induced functional cytokines, and TLR pathway signaling regulators, which work together to precisely balance the activation and inhibition of TLR signaling pathways (He et al., 2014). LncRNAs control TLR signaling pathways in a wider variety of ways than miRNAs do. To regulate TLR expression, lncRNAs can act as ceRNAs by concentrating on bound miRNAs (Ji et al., 2019). In addition, lncRNAs can specifically bind heterogenous nuclear ribonucleoprotein and positively or negatively regulate the transcription of immune response genes downstream of TLRs by binding to the gene promoters of TLR-induced immune response genes (Carpenter et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014). In contrast, circRNAs possesses a solitary regulatory mechanism and frequently function as a sponge RNA for miRNAs, potentially affecting TLR activation (Liu et al., 2024).

In summary, ncRNAs regulate TLRs and play important roles in the development of hydrocephalus by regulating various components of the TLR-NF-κB-SPAK-NKCC1 pathway and thereby inducing or inhibiting the development of hydrocephalus following a CNS infection or hemorrhage. Among ncRNAs, the relevant evidence for miRNAs is the most striking. Experiments conducted in vitro and in vivo on ICH rat brain tissue showed that miR-7 may mitigate LPS-induced microglial inflammatory responses and diminish neuroinflammation (Zhang et al., 2018). Coincidentally, it has also been shown that miR-140-5p adversely affects downstream MyD88/TRIF/NF-κB pathways and TLR4 in rats after ICH (Wang et al., 2019). The same is true for pathogen infections. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that Japanese encephalitis virus infection altered miRNA expression profiles, and KEGG analysis further validated the involvement of differential genes in TLR signaling pathways (Li et al., 2016). Target prediction analyses suggested that miR-155 matches tumor growth factor-β-activated kinase 1-binding protein 2, which inhibits increased levels of inflammatory factors and NF-κB activation caused by meningococcal Escherichia coli by promoting IL-1-dependent TRAF6 ubiquitination and IL-1 signaling complex assembly (Yang et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2023). Conversely, miR-146a has the ability to bind to either the IRAK1 3′ UTR or the TRAF6 3′ UTR. Moreover, antagomiR-155 and antagomiR-146a treatments further exacerbated microgliosis and shortened the survival time of mice with meningitic Escherichia coli infection (Yang et al., 2021). In an experimental model of SAH, miR-146a similarly suppressed inflammation by decreasing the gene production of inflammatory cytokines generated by hemoglobin through the IRAK1/TRAF6/NF-κB pathway (Liu et al., 2020). Conversely, miR-27a binds directly to TLR4 and IRAK4 3′ UTRs in the aforementioned signaling pathways to prevent their production. When LPS caused microglial inflammation, miR-27a expression was significantly downregulated, which resulted in the production of downstream inflammatory factors such TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 (Lv et al., 2017). Similar to this regulation, miR-367 also blocks IRAK4 expression by binding directly to its 3′ UTR, which in turn prevents NF-κB activation and the subsequent release of pro-inflammatory mediators. However, the study background for miR-367 was ICH, rather than bacterial infection. After ICH, primary microglia showed increased IRAK4 expression and decreased miR-367 expression, ultimately leading to increased inflammatory cytokine expression (Yuan et al., 2015). miRNAs are also critical for CPes, which are more importantly associated with hydrocephalus. miR-155 levels were increased and miR-223 and miR-181b expression were decreased in human CPes after IVH CSF-induced treatment in comparison with the corresponding levels in non-IVH samples (Fejes et al., 2021). An miRNA study of CSF samples from premature infants following IVH, however, contradicted this finding by demonstrating that the levels of miR-126, miR-155, miR-223, and miR-181b in CSF were elevated during the onset of the condition (Fejes et al., 2020). By targeting TRIF to block downstream NF-κB signaling pathways, dampen inflammatory cytokine expression, and reduce the generation of type I IFN, induction of miR-181b-2 can reduce excessive inflammation (Sun et al., 2021). Moreover, during infection, miR-155 can block NF-κB signaling to reduce inflammation (Cao et al., 2021). miR-223 can also regulate LPS-triggered inflammatory mediator expression by inhibiting TLR4-NF-κB signaling (Wang et al., 2015). MiR-155 reportedly seems to show more complex effects on TLR regulation. By focusing on Src homology 2-domain-containing inositol phosphatase-1 and suppressor of negative regulation of cytokine signaling, miR-155 enhances TLR4 activation. By triggering NF-κB, TLR4 activation can also raise the level of transcription of miR-155 (Guo et al., 2021). Consequently, more research is required to elucidate the precise mechanism of PIH and PHH regulation by the aforementioned miRNAs.

LncRNAs are also involved in the TLR-NF-κB-SPAK-NKCC1 pathway (Tripathi et al., 2021). After SAH, the brain tissues from SAH mice and the control group showed significantly different lncRNA and mRNA transcripts, according to a high-throughput sequencing bioinformatics analysis. The lncRNA/mRNA co-expression network indicates that BV-2 microglial inflammation as well as TLR4 transcription and translation were both reduced by fantom3F730004F19 knockdown (Peng et al., 2017). The functions of lncRNAs in CNS infections is even more unexpected. Meningitis induced by Escherichia coli is caused by overexpression of lncC11orf54-1, wherein translocated coil proteins break down to form mgU2-19 and mgU2-30. Furthermore, the ncRNA mgU2-30 stimulates IRAK1 autophosphorylation and oligomerization, which in turn activates NF-κB signaling and generates pro-inflammatory cytokines (Xu et al., 2022). Furthermore, NF-κB expression and brain water content in septic mice were markedly elevated by small interfering RNA (siRNA) interference with lncRNA nuclear paraspeckle assembly transcript 1 expression in the brain tissue (Liu et al., 2019). After Salmonella typhimurium infection, lncRNA TVX1 showed some protection against neuroinflammation in microglia. However, transfection with a lncRNA TVX1 overexpression plasmid raised IκB levels and lowered pp65 levels, providing more evidence that lncRNA TVX1 suppresses the NF-κB activation produced by Salmonella typhimurium (Zou et al., 2022).

The roles of circRNAs are not as well supported by data. In a rat model of SAH, circARF3 inhibited the MyD88/NF-κB pathway, attenuating the pro-inflammatory effects of miR-31-5p and lowering the production of TNF-α, IL-1β, and microglial inflammation (Cai et al., 2021).

Overall, the evidence indicates that in infectious or hemorrhagic diseases of the CNS, three types of ncRNAs cause hydrocephalus by regulating the TLR-NF-κB-SPAK-NKCC1 pathway, causing inflammatory responses in CPes and microglia, and increasing CSF secretion. However, these findings need to be further confirmed by more well-established experiments.

sec.title: Glymphatic pathways and aquaporin 4
sec.p: The distribution of aquaporins in the CNS is an important factor influencing their involvement in the pathophysiology of hydrocephalus. Aquaporins are widely distributed in the choroid plexus, astrocytes, neurons, cerebral cortex, cerebellum, oligodendrocytes, neural stem cells, and ependymal cells (Yang et al., 2022b; Xiao et al., 2023). We have primarily explained the findings for aquaporin 4 (AQP4) because it is intimately linked to the formation of hydrocephalus and the control of ncRNAs. A review of the glymphatic system may be useful to properly comprehend this concept. Because of the absence of lymphatic veins in the brain parenchyma, the brain was once believed to be the only organ in the human body devoid of lymphoid tissue. However, several studies have suggested that the brain has an essential network of extravascular channels that permit CSF and interstitial fluid (ISF) to pass across the CNS parenchyma and blood vessels (Carlstrom et al., 2022). Specifically, CSF enters from the perivascular space of perforating arteries, enters the interstitium through AQP4 on perivascular astrocytes, and then drives ISF and its solutes to drain into the perivenous space in order to complete CSF-ISF exchange and thus remove interstitial metabolic waste products; this pathway is traditionally referred to as the glymphatic pathway (Iliff et al., 2012; Plog and Nedergaard, 2018). More recently, multiple aspects related to CSF and ISF inflow channels, outflow channels, or both and their occurrence along arteries and/or veins have become topics of debate (Faghih and Sharp, 2018; Mestre et al., 2022). Studies have shown that the tracer flows along the basement membrane of smooth muscle cells in the arterial media to form an intramural periarterial drainage path for the elimination of ISF and metabolites in the brain (Albargothy et al., 2018). Similarly, the ISF and its constituent solutes (at least partially) are excreted into the subarachnoid CSF regardless of the perivascular route used (Klostranec et al., 2021). Thereafter, the CSF enters the cervical lymphatic system toward the frontal olfactory/cribriform region and posteriorly drains into the internal jugular venous system via cranial foramina of the skull base or dorsal dural lymphatics (Aspelund et al., 2015; Carlstrom et al., 2022). The glymphatic system mentioned above depends heavily on astrocyte AQP4, which mediates CSF-ISF exchange, for normal operation; APQ4 is concentrated in the perivascular astrocytic endfeet domains (Eidsvaag et al., 2017). The perivascular space of arteries, also known as the Virchow-Robin space, is where CSF enters the parenchymal space. It then passes via the glial basement membrane and astrocyte endfeet that surround the parenchyma of the brain (Rasmussen et al., 2018). To facilitate CSF outflow and ISF interaction, AQP4 of astrocyte endfeet decreases the resistance to CSF transport from the periarterial space to the interstitium and subsequently to the perivenous space (Plog and Nedergaard, 2018). Many studies have shown that AQP4 deletion or dysfunction can lead to glymphatic system dysfunction (Rasmussen et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2023). Experiments have shown that AQP4 gene-null mice had enlarged and arrested ISF and larger total brain volume due to reduced lymphatic clearance (Gomolka et al., 2023). MPTP-induced AQP4 polarization was impaired in PD mice, and decreased perivascular influx and efflux of CSF tracers further confirmed that AQP4 depolarization could lead to lymphatic dysfunction (Si et al., 2024).

The connection between AQP4 and hydrocephalus has been addressed in the existing research due to the significant function of AQP4 in brain water transport. AQP4 expression has been shown to increase following hydrocephalus formation, which may be a protective mechanism against CSF accumulation. Congenitally hydrocephalic H-Tx (hH-Tx) rats showed considerably higher levels of AQP4 expression in their cerebral cortex than normal rats; this discovery could be connected to the creation of additional CSF circulation routes (Shen et al., 2006). Both the amount of AQP4 mRNA in the rat brain and the amount of AQP4 immunoreactivity surrounding the vessels significantly increased in rats in which hydrocephalus was induced by injecting kaolin into the cisterna magna (Mao et al., 2006). Moreover, the AQP4 mRNA and protein levels increased on days 1 and 3 in a rat model of SAH-induced hydrocephalus (Long et al., 2019). The same conclusion was confirmed in hydrocephalus samples from patients (Skjolding et al., 2013). In another study of kaolin-induced hydrocephalus, the relative density of AQP4 in the cerebral cortex and periventricular area decreased significantly after 2 days, whereas periventricular AQP4 expression increased significantly after 2 weeks. Thus, AQP4 levels dynamically change in a time- and region-dependent manner in hydrocephalus formation (Skjolding et al., 2010). In a rat model of hydrocephalus established by autologous blood injection, silencing AQP4 aggravated hydrocephalus and caused dilated lateral ventricles, and this evidence further supports the above view (Guo et al., 2018). Moreover, glymphatic pathways and AQP4 can affect the course of some CNS diseases and have an indirect link with secondary hydrocephalus. Glymphatic system injury is one of the important pathogeneses of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) associated with Alzheimer’s disease (Reeves et al., 2020). Astrocytic endfoot membranes along cortical microvessels in iNPH patients have been reported to show considerably reduced AQP4 water channel density (Hasan-Olive et al., 2019). This finding may result in poor glymphatic circulation and obstructed waste elimination. In a related investigation, AQP4 immunoreactivity expression was found to be reduced in iNPH patients’ astrocytic perivascular endfeet and in certain areas of the neighboring neuropils (Eide and Hansson, 2018). Glymphatic pathway injury may also be closely associated with hydrocephalus caused by TBI. In a study conducted with a mouse TBI model, mice in the experimental group showed a 60% reduction in glymphatic pathway function in comparison with the control group, and this injury persisted for at least 1 month. Genetic knockout of AQP4 has been shown to aggravate glymphatic pathway dysfunction after TBI (Iliff et al., 2014). It has been shown that germinal matrix hemorrhage redistributes AQP4 from the paravascular space to the interstitial space and largely impairs CSF-ISF exchange in glymphatic pathways, resulting in hydrocephalus and ventricular enlargement (Ding et al., 2019). However, AQP4 expression has also been found to be positively correlated with hematoma and edema after ICH, which is diametrically opposite to the above protective effects (Zhong et al., 2013). Therefore, we believe that the glymphatic pathways and AQP4 play roles in ICH-induced PHH, but more studies are needed to elucidate the specific mechanisms.

Evidence has indicated that ncRNAs influence AQP4 and the glymphatic pathway in various diseases (Yaghoobi et al., 2024). MiR-130a has been shown to strongly suppress the AQP4 M1 promoter, which affects the expression of AQP4 in a dose-dependent manner (Sepramaniam et al., 2012). Patients with TBI showed considerably lower levels of miR-211-5p mRNA expression in their CSF, which was positively linked with the expression of matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9) and AQP4. The expression of MMP9 and AQP4 is increased by knockdown of miR-211-5p by inhibitors, which may represent a viable therapeutic strategy for the impairment of the glymphatic system following TBI (Wang et al., 2023a). Zhang et al. (2020) discovered that in a rat ICH model, glycine-histidine-lysine increased the levels of miR-146a-3p via the PI3K/Akt pathway, which in turn decreased astrocyte AQP4 expression, decreased brain water content, and ameliorated neurological impairments in ICH rats. In studies on mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease, intermittent fasting increased the levels of β-hydroxybutyrat, an endogenous histone deacetylase inhibitor, whereas β-hydroxybutyrat alleviated the decrease in miR-130a expression in aβ-exposed U251 cells (Sepramaniam et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2017). By blocking AQP4-M1 transcriptional activity and the modification of the AQP4-M1/M23 ratio in Alzheimer’s disease, miR-130a may lessen the loss of AQP4 polarity (Zhang et al., 2017). Furthermore, by lowering the expression of AQP4, NF-κB, and IL-6 after TBI, lncRNA Malat1 overexpression dramatically reduced brain edema in TBI rats (Zhang et al., 2019). Nevertheless, more data are required to validate the direct correlation between these ncRNAs and hydrocephalus.

sec.title: Non-Coding RNAs as Biomarkers of Hydrocephalus
sec.p: Hydrocephalus is commonly diagnosed using typical signs of ventricular dilatation on brain CT and MRI (Langner et al., 2017). Moreover, in premature infants, early cranial ultrasound-based quantitative ventricular evaluation can predict the need for CSF drainage in PHH (Obeid et al., 2019). However, biomarkers that can assess the occurrence and prognosis of hydrocephalus are still lacking. Several current studies combining high-throughput sequencing with bioinformatics analysis and animal experiments have screened potential biomarkers for the prediction of hydrocephalus (Wang et al., 2021c; Malhotra et al., 2023). As previously mentioned, Shi et al. (2019) used high-throughput sequencing to analyze the expression profiles of lncRNAs in mice with kaolin-induced hydrocephalus and controls. They discovered that a total of 1575 lncRNAs were differentially expressed in hydrocephalus models, with NONMMUT066583.2 and NONMMUT070521.2 being the most upregulated and downregulated lncRNA transcripts. These transcripts are expected to be biomarkers of hydrocephalus (Shi et al., 2019). As previously indicated, upregulation of hsa-miR-130b-3p in CSF exosomes may serve as a prognostic target for CH (Chen et al., 2022). Coincidentally, Spaull et al. (2019) detected enrichment of miR-9, miR-17, miR-26a, miR-124, and miR-1911 in CSF exosomes from premature infants with PHH, and their expression changed over time; this finding is expected to provide optional biomarkers for PHH in premature infants. In addition, the detection of CSF hsa-miR-4274 expression levels is expected to be useful to distinguish Alzheimer’s disease, iNPH, and Parkinsonism and thereby confirm the diagnosis and predict the expected effects of CSF shunt therapy (Jurjević et al., 2017). For the diagnosis and prognosis of conditions like SAH, ICH, and CNS infection—diseases that are intimately linked to the occurrence of hydrocephalus—ncRNAs are more helpful (Zhan et al., 2020; Kim and Chae, 2022; Huang et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2024; Table 2).

sec.title: Non-Coding RNAs as Therapeutic Targets for Hydrocephalus
Interventional approaches
sec.p: miRNA mimics, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small-molecule inhibitors, and miRNA sponges are the primary techniques used at present to obstruct endogenous miRNA pathways (Winkle et al., 2021). miRNA mimics are roughly dsRNA ~21 nt in length, and the majority of them link to the Argonaute protein to create an RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) that silences target genes (Wang et al., 2021b). In contrast to miRNA mimics, ASOs are single-stranded, typically 12–30 nucleotides long, and they bind to target RNAs selectively using the Watson–Crick base pairing rules. ASOs regulate gene expression through either an occupancy-only antisense mechanism or an RNA cleavage antisense mechanism (Bennett, 2019). Small-molecule inhibitors negatively regulate miRNAs in four main ways: (1) directly binding to mature miRNAs; (2) binding to functional sites associated with miRNA processing in miRNA precursors; (3) blocking the assembly of miRNA precursors; and (4) blocking the formation of miRNA-induced silencing complexes (Sun et al., 2023). Small-molecule inhibitors can be developed by computational prediction, high-throughput experimental screening, and a hybrid method for computational prediction and experimental screening (Liu et al., 2021a). MiRNA sponges, also known as ceRNAs, competitively bind miRNAs, thereby relieving mRNA inhibition by specific miRNAs. miRNAs mainly include endogenously transcribed pseudogenes, lncRNAs, circRNAs, and viral miRNA sponges (Bak and Mikkelsen, 2014).

Targeted regulation by lncRNAs occurs partly in the same manner as miRNAs, such as ASOs, small-molecule compounds, and the underlying principle is also much the same as that in miRNA regulation. In addition, siRNAs and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) technology are also popular lncRNA-targeting methods at present (Chen et al., 2021a). siRNAs are long double-stranded RNA molecules of 21–23 nucleotides that act by degrading mRNA after transcription. Specifically, siRNAs bind a ribonucleoprotein called RISC within the cytoplasm upon entry into cells. The guided strand remains stable because of the presence of ARGO protein, while the follower strand is degraded. The activated RISC eventually binds complementarily to the targeting RNA and induces its degradation. At present, this technology has been applied to target lncRNAs, but its stability and accuracy require further improvement (Pang et al., 2020; Alshaer et al., 2021). The CRISPR-CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) system includes two parts: a single-guide RNA or CRISPR RNA (crRNA)-trans-activating CRISPR RN structure synthesized by the genome engineering mechanism and Cas9 endonuclease. Among these, single-guide RNAs direct the Cas9 endonuclease to specific DNA sequences in the genome, and Cas9 cleaves to produce double-strand breaks, which are later repaired by host-mediated DNA repair mechanisms (Jiang and Doudna, 2017). However, CRISPR/Cas9 technology targeting lncRNAs is currently limited to basic research and has been poorly studied in hydrocephalus and related diseases.

Targeted regulation of circRNAs appears to be a more promising therapeutic modality. In addition to the previously described siRNAs and CRISPR/Cas9, short hairpin RNA (shRNA) and Cas13 systems targeting RNA have now been used to induce circRNA silencing in specific tissues (Misir et al., 2022). ShRNA matures in a different manner than siRNA but is similarly dependent on ARGO protein containing RISC, thereby cleaving and degrading target RNAs or providing RNA interference through translational inhibition via p-bodies (Rao et al., 2009). The Cas13 enzyme has two higher eukaryote and prokaryote nucleotide-binding endoRNase domains that mediate more precise RNA cleavage than CRISPR/Cas9. This form of precise nucleic acid editing offers the possibility of developing new gene therapies (Cox et al., 2017). CircRNA still lacks clear applications in hydrocephalus and related diseases, and further exploration is expected.

sec.title: Delivery systems
sec.p: The regulation modes described above need to be safely and effectively delivered into the CNS to have the corresponding effects. ASOs, ncRNA mimics, small-molecule inhibitors, ceRNAs, and siRNAs are delivered in the CNS by direct injection and delivery using vectors. Among these techniques, direct injection can be performed by intracerebroventricular or intranasal injections (Wang et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2020). Carrier delivery is more stable, specific, cell-permeable, and less immunogenic than direct injection (Chen et al., 2021a). Commonly used delivery vectors include exosomes, lipid nanoparticles, and viral vectors (e.g., lentiviruses and adenoviruses). Modified and purified exosomes can be loaded with mimics or inhibitors of ncRNAs and transported to specific tissues or organs to exert therapeutic effects (Li et al., 2021). Because of their superior biocompatibility and biodegradability, lipid nanoparticles are more suitable for the delivery of small molecules in the CNS. However, the complexity of the fabrication process, the mechanism of liver uptake, and the process of crossing the blood–brain barrier pose challenges for the widespread promotion of lipid nanoparticles (Khare et al., 2023). Viral vectors mainly include lentiviral vectors and adenoviral vectors, both of which have been demonstrated to act as vectors for ncRNAs, but their safety is controversial and therefore gradually replaced by non-viral vectors (Savenkova et al., 2022).

sec.title: Non-coding RNAs in the treatment of hydrocephalus and associated diseases
Post–traumatic brain injury hydrocephalus
sec.p: Previous studies have demonstrated that some ncRNA mimics, inhibitors, and drugs influence the inflammatory response after TBI by targeting ncRNAs. For instance, Si et al. (2020) observed that in a mouse model of TBI, the administration of an miR-193a hairpin inhibitor (antagomir) prevented the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and markedly decreased the production of pro-inflammatory markers such CD68, IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and COX-2. In an experimental study, Wang et al. (2021c) observed that delivering miR-146a-containing nanoparticles into the human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y and microglial BV-2 cell lines dramatically decreased TRAF6 and IRAK1 expression, which in turn preented the activation of the NF-κB pathway. In TBI model cells, the miR-29a-5p mimic binds to the NLRP3 3′ UTR and adversely controls its expression (Zhang et al., 2021). TBI mice exhibit elevated expression of the long ncRNA KCNQ1 antisense transcript 1 (KCNQ1OT1); inhibition of KCNQ1OT1 can regulate the miR-873-5p-TRAF6-p38/NF-κB axis, which is neuroprotective in TBI mice; it can also target the 3′ UTR of TRAF6 and inhibit microglial inflammatory responses, which in turn lowers the expression of pro-inflammatory factors such as IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α (Liu et al., 2021b). RnocircRNA_010705 (circLrp1b) increases Dram2 expression and acts as a sponge for miR-27a-3p to induce autophagy and inflammation in TBI. Dexmedetomidine functions as a protective agent by inhibiting the circLrp1b/miR-27a3p/Dram2 signaling pathway (Li et al., 2020). We summarized the potential to achieve prevention and treatment of hydrocephalus after TBI by targeting current pathways and key molecules that may lead to post–traumatic brain injury hydrocephalus through techniques that regulate ncRNAs. However, more studies are needed to verify the direct protective effect of the above techniques on post–traumatic brain injury hydrocephalus.

sec.title: Post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus
sec.p: Schizandrin A has been demonstrated to significantly attenuate SAH-induced neuroinflammation by inhibiting the miR-155/NF-κB axis and downregulating the expression of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 (Jin et al., 2024). Peripheral injection of exosomes loaded with miR-193b-3p (Exos) into the brains of mice with SAH has also been shown to reduce the inflammatory response by acetylating NF-κB p65 and inhibiting HDAC3 expression and activity (Lai et al., 2020). In a cellular model of SAH, delivery of miR-140-5p via microglial EV downregulated monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation and suppressed the PI3K/AKT and Erk1/2 pathways, thereby inhibiting microglial activation and secretion of TNF-α and IL-1β (Wang et al., 2023b). Qu et al. (2019) constructed a rat model of ICH and injected miR-146a, which mimics the process of intracerebroventricular hemorrhage. The findings demonstrated that miR-146a inhibited oxidative stress, greatly reduced the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the brain tissue of rats with ICH, and targeted the TRAF6/NF-κB pathway. However, the application of lncRNAs and circRNAs in PHH needs to be explored.

sec.title: Post-infectious hydrocephalus
sec.p: Drugs, miRNA mimics, miRNA inhibitors, miRNA-loaded exosomes, and extracellular vesicles all contribute to the inhibition of neuroinflammation following ICH. Oral administration of the dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor alogliptin has been shown to significantly rescue the LPS-induced increase in miR-155 gene expression, decrease TNF-α and IL-6 levels after LPS induction, and significantly inhibit TLR4 and MyD88 protein expression and NF-κB p65 content in the brain following intracerebroventricular injection of LPS (El-Sahar et al., 2021). Coincidentally, propofol has been demonstrated to suppress miR-155 expression in BV2 microglia after LPS treatment, thereby upregulating the suppressor of negative regulation of cytokine signaling, a downstream target of miR-155, and suppressing inflammatory responses in microglia (Zheng et al., 2018). In a study performed with lncRNA, propofol was found to downregulate the expression of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β in LPS-stimulated astrocytes by inhibiting lncRNA-MEG3, thereby reducing NF-κB activity and inhibiting its activation through phosphorylation (Zhang et al., 2022c). Similarly, further studies are expected to confirm the direct effects of these agents on the treatment of PIH.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This review had some limitations. Because of the limited direct experimental evidence for ncRNAs and hydrocephalus, some of the conclusions in this paper are based on the conclusion that ncRNAs are relevant for diseases that can be secondary to hydrocephalus or are consistent with the pathophysiological mechanisms of hydrocephalus. Nevertheless, the primary objective of this review is to highlight potential future directions for studying hydrocephalus. Some of the views in the article require confirmation in future studies.

sec.title: Conclusions and Prospects
sec.p: Hydrocephalus is a life-threatening CNS disease with a complex range of causes, diverse clinical manifestations, and pathophysiological mechanisms that require elucidation. At present, ventriculo-peritoneal shunting, ETV and some drugs are mainly used to treat hydrocephalus in clinical practice, but these modalities are associated with undesirable complications such as infection, bleeding and obstruction. These limitations highlight the need for further exploration of the pathophysiological and molecular mechanisms of hydrocephalus formation.

NcRNAs mainly include miRNAs, lncRNAs, and circRNA, which can regulate gene expression or interact to form a regulatory network by regulating transcriptional activity and epigenetic modifications, affecting pre-mRNA splicing, inducing mRNA degradation, inhibiting translation, and acting as ceRNA. The development of high-throughput sequencing technology has revealed that patients with hydrocephalus show some changes in ncRNA expression profiles.

On this basis, this paper comprehensively reviews the regulatory mechanisms of ncRNAs in hydrocephalus and diseases closely related to hydrocephalus (SAH, ICH, CNS infection, TBI, congenital CNS and choroid plexus developmental defects, and Alzheimer’s disease). ncRNAs are mainly involved in the pathophysiological process of hydrocephalus by regulating CNS development and choroid plexus ciliogenesis-related pathways, targeting NLRP3 inflammasomes and TLR-NFκB pathways to regulate CSF secretion, and affecting the glymphatic pathway by regulating AQP4. In addition, the potential of ncRNAs as biomarkers of hydrocephalus and in the development of more valuable therapeutic agents has been addressed in the existing research.

Nevertheless, the existing understanding of the relationship between ncRNAs and hydrocephalus, as well as related diseases, represents only the tip of the iceberg. Additional animal and clinical trials are needed to verify the specific regulatory mechanisms. The feasibility of some emerging gene therapy methods targeting ncRNAs, such as CRISPR/Cas9, CRISPR/Cas13 and shRNA, in the treatment of hydrocephalus and related diseases requires further investigation. We look forward to the use of these ncRNAs for hydrocephalus, which will provide novel perspectives for the development of treatment strategies for hydrocephalus.
